title: Obese, disabled man suffocated after being handcuffed, medical examiner report shows
subtitle: The mother of a man who suffocated after being handcuffed and left alone in a police van last year in Edmonton wants officers to know more about the potentially fatal consequences of such actions on obese people. An autopsy report by Medical Examiner Dr. Bernard Bannach on Trevor Proudman found the 32-year-old man died in part as a result of being handcuffed with his wrists behind his back. His numerous medical conditions contributed to making that position fatal.
article: The mother of an Edmonton man who suffocated after being handcuffed and left alone in a police van last year wants officers to know more about the potentially fatal consequences of such actions on obese people.

An autopsy report by Medical Examiner Dr. Bernard Bannach found 32-year-old Trevor Proudman died in part due to being handcuffed with his wrists behind his back. His numerous medical conditions contributed to making that position fatal.
"This position did not allow him to breathe adequately, resulting in a cardiac arrest," the report says.

Proudman weighed 280 pounds and stood approximately five-feet, four-inches tall. He had a genetic defect called Prader Willi syndrome, which results in intense food cravings. Proudman also had sleep apnea and scoliosis, a curvature in his spine. He had a relatively small chest cavity resulting from these conditions, making it difficult to breathe with his hands behind his back.
"I just hope they make changes. They need to have some training. A larger person ... why even handcuff them? And they should never be left alone," Proudman's mother, Maureen Warren, said Thursday.
"They probably didn't know ... But just seeing the size of him. Laying a bigger person down? It seems like it should be common sense to me. There was no common sense."

Police were called to a medical clinic near 122nd Avenue and 97th Street on Nov. 12, 2014, after clinic staff called about a man acting aggressively. Prader Willi syndrome also causes developmental delays and reduced mental capacity.
Proudman was handcuffed and placed in a police van on his side, while two officers interviewed people inside the clinic.
When Warren arrived at the clinic, she was told her son was still in the van. After waiting several minutes for officers to bring him out, she started to panic.
"We thought, 'What is going on?' Then we saw the paddy wagon bouncing and that's when we ran around the back. They were doing CPR and his face was blue."

Warren has seen the widely publicized death of Eric Garner, whose arrest by New York City police was videotaped. Garner, an obese man, was killed by "compression of neck (choke hold), compression of chest and prone positioning during physical restraint by police," an autopsy found. Garner was heard repeatedly telling officers, "I can't breathe."
An officer involved in the incident was not indicted, spurring widespread protests.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, which looks into deaths or shootings in which police are involved, said it is reviewing the EPS investigation into the incident.
"I think charges should be laid, but I'm sure they won't," Warren said. "They need a group of people who are not police to review things."
Warren said her son had contact with police on several occasions before he died. She wondered why information on his condition was not on his file when police arrived.
The incident was a "tragedy," EPS spokeswoman Cheryl Sheppard said in an email.
"The Edmonton Police Service is interested in understanding the causes behind his death," she said, but declined to comment further because ASIRT is investigating.
